1037.title: Easter Monday
1037.hook: a day for walking, like Emmaus; in some places the Emmaus walk
1037.howItsDone: In some places Christians keep Easter Monday with an Emmaus walk, going out together on foot after the feast, and some churches read Luke's Emmaus story in the days after Easter.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Orthodox Pascha: a midnight call, an answer, and red eggs. Your line was truly he is risen.

Two friends are walking out of Jerusalem, late in the day, toward a village called Emmaus. They're going over it all: the arrest, the cross, and that morning's strange report from some women of an empty tomb. A stranger falls into step and asks what they're talking about. They stop, faces sad, and Cleopas more or less says: are you the only person around here who hasn't heard? He lets them tell it. Then he starts to talk, and the road gets shorter. Some places keep the day after Easter just like this, with a walk. Today, Easter Monday.

Luke is careful about one detail: this happens on Easter day itself. So why does a Monday borrow it? Because the morning after a great feast is when ordinary life starts again, and this is Easter turning up on an ordinary road. In the King James Bible: "Jesus himself drew near, and went with them." But Luke says their eyes were held. He walks the whole way as a stranger, going through Moses and the prophets, explaining the things written about himself. At the village he makes as if to keep walking, and they press him: "Abide with us: for it is toward evening, and the day is far spent." So he comes in. At the table he takes bread, blesses it, breaks it and hands it to them, and they know him. Then he's gone from their sight. And they say to each other: "Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way, and while he opened to us the scriptures?" They knew him at the table, but the burning started on the road. Readers find layers here. Some hear an echo of communion in the breaking of bread. Some hear the risen Christ walking beside people who don't yet see him. Others notice the plain hospitality: two tired travelers invite a stranger in at dusk. Then the last turn. That same hour they hurry back to Jerusalem to tell the others how he was "known of them in breaking of bread."
screen: `THAT SAME DAY, ON AN ORDINARY ROAD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person you could walk beside, not to fix anything, just to talk, and picture the route: a park, the long way to the shop. Leave a gap in the talk you imagine, because the Emmaus story happens in the gap nobody planned. If you pray, ask that the road be good company; if you don't, just hold that person in mind.
Easter Monday. The day after Easter, kept in some places with a walk, remembering the road to Emmaus and the stranger who turned out to be the risen Jesus.
Your line: walk to Emmaus. Their hearts burned long before they knew why. Thanks for sitting with me.

1038.title: Thomas Sunday
1038.hook: the Sunday after Easter remembers Thomas; Catholics also keep Divine Mercy Sunday
1038.howItsDone: In a number of churches, John 20's story of Thomas is read on the Sunday after Easter; the Orthodox call it Thomas Sunday, and Catholics also keep it as Divine Mercy Sunday.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Easter Monday: two friends on the road who didn't know who was walking with them. Your line was walk to Emmaus.

Thomas was out when it happened. His friends find him and tell him they've seen Jesus alive, and he answers them plainly. In the King James Bible: "Except I shall see in his hands the print of the nails, and put my finger into the print of the nails, and thrust my hand into his side, I will not believe." He isn't rude about it. He just says what it would take. Nothing secondhand. For eight days the story leaves him there, the one in the room who can't say what everyone else is saying. In the Orthodox calendar, the Sunday after Easter is named for him. Today, Thomas Sunday.

John tells it: "after eight days again his disciples were within, and Thomas with them." Doors shut. Jesus stands among them and says, "Peace be unto you." Then he turns to Thomas and offers exactly what he asked for: "Reach hither thy finger, and behold my hands; and reach hither thy hand, and thrust it into my side: and be not faithless, but believing." Notice two things. Jesus doesn't refuse the request; he answers it almost word for word. And John never says Thomas actually touched him. Some paintings show his finger in the wound, but the text goes straight to what he says: "My Lord and my God." The one who doubted out loud is the one who says it, face to face. Then a line for everyone who wasn't in that room: "blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed." Remember who Thomas was before this, too. Earlier in John, when Jesus decides to go back toward danger, it's Thomas who tells the others, "Let us also go, that we may die with him." The nickname doubting Thomas isn't in the Bible. Some readers would rather say honest Thomas, or brave Thomas. Catholics also keep this Sunday as Divine Mercy Sunday, a day centered on God's mercy, and some hear the two fitting together: a wounded Christ, offering peace, to a friend who couldn't yet believe.

Let one honest question come up, about faith or about anything you're asked to trust, and don't argue it down or polish it. Say it to yourself plainly, the way Thomas did, with your terms: this is what it would take. If you pray, bring that doubt to God just as it is; if you don't, hold the question with a bit of respect, as a sign you're paying attention.
Thomas Sunday. The Sunday after Easter, remembering the disciple who said what it would take to believe, and then said, my Lord and my God.
Your line: my Lord and my God. A doubt said out loud, and answered. Day one thousand thirty-eight, done.

1039.title: Rogation days
1039.hook: villages walk their boundaries praying for the crops
1039.howItsDone: On Rogation days some parishes walk their boundaries in procession, stopping at markers to read scripture and pray for the crops and the community; some city churches walk their streets instead.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Thomas Sunday: a doubt said out loud, answered, and then the words of your line, my Lord and my God.

A stone sits half sunk in a hedge at the edge of a field, its letters worn almost smooth. On a set day, in some English villages, a crowd turns up beside it: the priest, the farmers, children carrying long willow sticks. They've walked since morning, field to field, stopping at every marker where their parish ends. At each one, someone reads, someone prays for the crops, and the children whack the stone so they'll remember where it is. In the old stories, sometimes it was the children who got bumped on it. The custom has a blunt name: beating the bounds. The days it belongs to have a gentler one. Today, Rogation days.

Tradition explains the name from the Latin for asking, and asking is the whole point: rain at the right time, sun at the right time, a harvest, the things a village can't make for itself. Two old lines fit the day. A psalm, in the King James Bible: "Then shall the earth yield her increase; and God, even our own God, shall bless us." And Jesus's plain invitation: "Ask, and it shall be given you." A town that grows its own food knows how little of it is in human hands, and Rogation says so out loud, on foot, in the fields. Why walk the boundary? Partly memory: the line lived in people's heads, so the young had to see the stones. But there's a moral edge too. Deuteronomy says: "Thou shalt not remove thy neighbour's landmark, which they of old time have set in thine inheritance." A boundary stone protects the person on the other side as much as you. Walking it and praying at it says: this much is ours to tend, that much is our neighbor's, and we won't creep. So beating the bounds holds two things together: asking God for enough, and honoring where enough ends. Some churches still walk their parish, in the country or around city blocks, praying for the homes, shops and gardens they pass, and for the people who work the land everywhere.

Start at your own front door and walk to the corner in your mind, picturing who lives along the way, the shop, the tree, the patch where something grows. At each corner, stop: if you pray, ask for what that stretch needs, work, rest, food on the table, peace between the houses; if you don't, just wish each stretch well as you pass it.
Rogation days. Days of asking, when some parishes walk their boundaries, praying for the crops and for the people inside the line and beyond it.
Your line: beating the bounds. A stone that guards your neighbor as much as you. That's day one thousand thirty-nine.

1040.title: Ascension Day
1040.howItsDone: Churches that keep Ascension Day mark it forty days after Easter with a service reading the end of Luke and the start of Acts; some move the celebration to the following Sunday.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rogation days: walking the edges and asking for the harvest. Your line was beating the bounds.

A small group of friends stands on a hill outside Jerusalem, heads tipped back, staring at an empty sky. A moment ago Jesus was talking with them. Then he was lifted up, and a cloud took him out of their sight. It's the stance of someone left on a platform after the train has gone. Then two men in white are beside them, and in the King James Bible they ask a fair question: "Ye men of Galilee, why stand ye gazing up into heaven?" Acts sets this after forty days of Jesus appearing to his friends. Today, Ascension Day.

Acts says the risen Jesus was "seen of them forty days, and speaking of the things pertaining to the kingdom of God." That's where the feast's timing comes from. Then the hill: "while they beheld, he was taken up; and a cloud received him out of their sight." In the Bible a cloud can be more than weather. It's how God's presence shows up and hides at once, over the mountain, over the tent in the desert. So the cloud isn't saying he got lost in the sky. Christians say he went into God's presence, and the old creeds say it too: he ascended into heaven, and sits at the right hand of the Father. Churches understand that differently, some picturing an upward journey, some hearing "up" as the only word we have for going into God. Either way, in the texts it isn't a goodbye. Luke ends his Gospel: "they worshipped him, and returned to Jerusalem with great joy." Not grief. Joy. Set that beside Matthew, who doesn't tell the Ascension at all and ends with a promise: "lo, I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world." Some Christians put it this way: at the Ascension, Jesus stops being in one place so he can be with his friends everywhere. Then the angels' question does its work. Stop staring up. Go back to the city. There's a wait coming, and then a job. Look up, then get on with it.

Go to a window or step outside if you can, look up at whatever's there, sky, ceiling, clouds, and let your shoulders drop. If you pray, hold Matthew's line in the quiet, lo, I am with you alway; if you don't, notice the size of the sky over your small day. Then bring your eyes down to the next ordinary thing in front of you.
Ascension Day. Forty days after Easter, the feast of Jesus taken up into God's presence, and the promise that he stays with his friends.
Your line: he is with you always. They went back to the city with joy, not grief. See you tomorrow.

1041.title: Pentecost in red
1041.hook: churches wear red, some read Acts in many languages at once
1041.howItsDone: At Pentecost some churches use red vestments and decorations, and some invite readers to read Acts 2 aloud in several languages at once.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ascension Day: a cloud, a hill, and friends told to stop staring at the sky. Your line was he is with you always.

The reader steps up to the lectern on Pentecost Sunday and starts the story in English. A moment later a second voice joins in, in Spanish. Then a third, in Korean. A fourth, in Swahili. A fifth, in something nobody in the third row can place. For a few seconds the church is a wonderful mess of sound, some catching their own language somewhere in the noise. And the room has gone red: red stoles, red banners, people in red shirts and scarves. Some churches do exactly this, on purpose. They're acting out a story. Today, Pentecost in red.

It's in the second chapter of Acts. Jesus's friends are together in one room, waiting, as they were told. In the King James Bible: "suddenly there came a sound from heaven as of a rushing mighty wind, and it filled all the house where they were sitting. And there appeared unto them cloven tongues like as of fire, and it sat upon each of them." That's the red: fire, resting on each person. Then they begin "to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance." The word does double duty. Tongues of fire on their heads; tongues, meaning languages, in their mouths. In the street, people from many nations gather, baffled, because "every man heard them speak in his own language." They ask, "how hear we every man in our own tongue, wherein we were born?" Notice what doesn't happen. The Spirit doesn't hand everyone one shared language. Nobody has to give up their mother tongue to understand. Some readers hear an answer to the tower of Babel, where languages scattered people: here the languages stay, and people are gathered anyway. Not everybody's impressed. Some mock and say they're "full of new wine." That's why some churches read Acts in several languages at once on this day: the jumble is the point. And it's why the red. Acts tells this as the day the Spirit came like fire, and churches that keep the color dress the room to look like it.
screen: `TONGUES ON THEIR HEADS, AND IN THEIR MOUTHS.`

segments.voice: Hold something red, a sock, a pen, a mug, and let the color stand for the fire in the story. Bring to mind someone whose first language isn't yours, a neighbor, a coworker, and think of the words they grew up with. If you pray, hold that person before God in their own tongue, without knowing a word of it; if you don't, just honor the language they carry.
Glossa. Greek for tongue, meaning language too, the word behind the fire and the many languages the Spirit gave at Pentecost.
Your line: every tongue. Nobody had to give up their own to understand. Day one thousand forty-one, done.

1042.title: Trinity Sunday
1042.hook: the one Sunday for the mystery at the heart of it all
1042.howItsDone: On Trinity Sunday some churches sing hymns to the Trinity and say a creed, and preachers often take up the texts where Father, Son and Spirit are named together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, glossa: wind, fire, and a crowd hearing the news in their own languages. Your line was every tongue.

A legend is told about Augustine, the North African bishop and writer. He's walking a beach, turning over a hard question: how can God be one, and also three? He finds a child running to the sea with a shell, pouring water into a little hole in the sand. What are you doing? Putting the sea in this hole. Augustine laughs: that's impossible. And the child answers, more or less, so is fitting God into your head. The legend doesn't need to be true to land. After Easter and Pentecost, the calendar keeps one Sunday just for that question. Today, Trinity Sunday.
screen: `THE SEA IN A HOLE IN THE SAND.`

segments.voice: Start with one God. Moses says it in Deuteronomy, in the King James Bible: "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD." Jesus quotes it himself when asked which commandment comes first. And yet the Gospels keep naming three together. At Jesus's baptism in Matthew, the Spirit comes down like a dove, and a voice from heaven says, "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." Father speaking, Son in the water, Spirit descending, in one scene. At the end of Matthew, Jesus sends his friends out "baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost." Some Christian readers point out: the name, not the names. And Paul signs off a letter: "The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Ghost, be with you all." Over time the church found a word for what these texts hold together: Trinity. One God, say Christians who hold the creeds, in three persons. Not three gods. Not one God wearing three masks. Father, Son and Spirit, each fully God, and one. Some teachers say every picture falls short: shamrocks, water and ice and steam help a little, then leak. That's why Christians call it a mystery: not a puzzle awaiting a clever answer, but something held true that you can live inside without reaching the bottom. The sea doesn't fit in the hole. People still swim in it.
screen: `THE LORD OUR GOD IS ONE LORD.`
`FATHER, SON AND SPIRIT IN ONE SCENE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something you know is true but can't fully explain: the way a parent loves three children completely, or what a person is, really, behind the face. If you pray, rest in Paul's farewell, the grace of Christ, the love of God, the communion of the Spirit; if you don't, let the big thing stay big, and sit beside it.
Trinity Sunday. The Sunday after Pentecost, for the Christian belief in one God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit: in Christian words, a mystery, not a puzzle.
Your line: three in one. Some things are for living inside, not for solving. That's day one thousand forty-two.

1043.title: Corpus Christi
1043.hook: Catholics carry the sacrament through the streets in procession
1043.howItsDone: On Corpus Christi some Catholic parishes carry the consecrated host in a monstrance through the streets under a canopy, with hymns, candles and stops for prayer along the way.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Trinity Sunday: the sea that won't fit in a hole. Your line was three in one.

A small bell rings at the corner, and the street goes quiet. Down the road, over a carpet of petals someone spent all night laying out, comes a procession: children in white, a band, candles, and under a canopy on poles, a priest holding something gold and shining. In its center is a small round wafer of bread. As it passes, people on the sidewalk kneel. A man on a bike takes off his cap. This happens in some Catholic towns and parishes on one feast, whose name is just two Latin words. Today, Corpus Christi.
screen: `A BELL, AND THE STREET GOES QUIET.`

segments.voice: Corpus Christi is Latin for the body of Christ. The words go back to the night before Jesus died. Paul passes them on, in the King James Bible: Jesus took bread, gave thanks, broke it, and said, "this is my body, which is broken for you: this do in remembrance of me." In John, Jesus says, "I am the living bread which came down from heaven." Christians understand those words in more than one way. Catholic teaching holds that at Mass the bread truly becomes the body of Christ, and that he remains present in it afterward. So the consecrated host can be kept, honored and carried, and on this feast it goes out through the streets. Orthodox Christians also speak of the bread truly becoming Christ's body, though this procession belongs to the Western calendar, and some Anglican churches mark the day too. Other Protestants understand communion as a remembrance, or as Christ present by the Spirit to those who receive it, and wouldn't carry the bread in procession. Each takes the words seriously; they hear them differently. For those who keep it, the procession says: what happens at the altar isn't meant to stay behind the church doors. It goes past the bakery and the bus stop. That fits the week: two friends who knew him in the breaking of bread at Emmaus, a parish walking its boundaries, a street crowd hearing the news in their own languages. Again and again, the holy went outside.

Walk your streets in your mind, pausing as a procession does: the busiest place you pass in a week, a station or a supermarket line; then a quiet one, a clinic waiting room; then the place you'll be tonight. If you pray, pray for the people in each place, as the procession blesses its streets; if you don't, hold each place as if it mattered, because to someone it does.
Corpus Christi. Latin for the body of Christ: a feast when Catholics carry the consecrated bread out of the church and through the streets.
